title: Tangled Inheritance (Multi-Dimensional Type Specialization)
pattern: An inheritance hierarchy or concrete struct tree attempts to represent variations along two or more completely independent dimensions simultaneously (e.g., Deal State and Presentation Layout), leading to a combinatorial explosion of types.
why_bad: Adding a new variant along one dimension (e.g., adding a `Graphed` presentation layout) requires manually writing types for all variants in the other dimension (`GraphedActiveDeal`, `GraphedPassiveDeal`), causing massive duplication and making changes highly expensive.
detection: Structs whose names combine adjectives from different dimensions of variation (e.g., `Tabular` + `Active`, `Single` + `Passive`).
counterexample: Unified, simple decorators that wrap objects sequentially to add transient capabilities without defining combinatorial static type trees.
fix: Apply delegation (Tease Apart Inheritance). Create two independent, simple hierarchies or trait structures (e.g., `DealState` and `LayoutRenderer`) and have the primary type compose them via delegation.
source: Martin Fowler, *Refactoring*, Chapter 12 ("Tease Apart Inheritance"), p. 507; Sandi Metz, *Practical Object-Oriented Design* (2019), Chapter 6.
